text: Before you use the dashboard, identify the conditions inside the pot.
title: Start inside the pot

text: What do the roots need?
title: What do roots need?

text: Picture a handful of gravel. The pieces are solid, but there are gaps between them. A pot also contains solid material and spaces. The growing material around the roots is called substrate; coco and stone wool are examples.
title: Substrate, water and air

visual.alt: Conceptual pot cutaway: solid substrate, held water, air spaces and roots.

text: Those spaces can contain water or air. Roots take up water, and they also need oxygen. Filling every space with water leaves less room for air.
title: Spaces hold water or air

visual.alt: Conceptual pot cutaway: solid substrate, held water, air spaces and roots.

text: So pouring in more water is not always helpful. The substrate needs to hold water, let excess drain away, and allow air back into some spaces.
title: Hold water. Drain excess. Allow air.

visual.alt: Conceptual pot cutaway: solid substrate, held water, air spaces and roots.

text: Look at the spare container. Water enters the substrate. Some water stays in the substrate. Other water drains into the tray.
title: Follow the water

visual.alt: Example paths: delivered water can remain, drain, or leave through roots and evaporation.

text: The amount of water then decreases. The plant uses some water. Evaporation and drainage also remove water.
title: Three ways water leaves

visual.alt: Example paths: delivered water can remain, drain, or leave through roots and evaporation.

text: A decrease in water content does not show only the water that the plant used.
title: Water loss has several causes

visual.alt: Example paths: delivered water can remain, drain, or leave through roots and evaporation.

text: This pot stays very wet. The leaves look unhealthy. Does this mean that you must add more water?
title: Very wet: add more water?

text: Choose one answer. Add more water immediately. Or do a check to find the cause first.
title: Choose the next action

text: Do a check first.
title: Check the cause first

text: Different problems can cause similar symptoms. The graph gives useful information. It does not identify every problem in the roots.
title: One symptom can have several causes

text: Think of driving a car: you make adjustments to keep it on course. Crop steering means adjusting growing conditions to influence growth. Here we focus on irrigation, which means supplying water to the crop.
title: Steer growing conditions

text: With irrigation, you choose when water arrives, how much arrives, and how long to wait before the next delivery. Light, temperature and humidity also change how much water the crop needs.
title: Delivery settings and water demand

text: Later we will name two steering directions: vegetative and generative. They describe management intended to influence leafy growth or reproductive development. Neither guarantees yield. Drying the pot as much as possible is not the goal; roots must keep working.
title: Steering must support working roots

visual.alt: Local probe region: check the exact quantity, location and age.

text: A thermometer in one room cannot tell you the temperature in every room. A moisture sensor has the same local limit: one reading does not describe every pot or prove every dripper is clear.
title: Like a thermometer in one room

visual.alt: Local probe region: check the exact quantity, location and age.

text: Use sensor readings with equipment checks and crop observations.
title: Use three kinds of evidence

text: Practise in the demo first; it does not operate a real pump. For a new installation, start with one zone: a group of plants whose water delivery is controlled together.
